To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) CNNs are a promising technique for CADe; (b) CNN models with a large number of layers, and a high number of parameters, perform better than those with fewer layers and parameters; (c) the performance of CNNs can be significantly improved by using large scale annotated datasets; (d) the use of spatial context information in training CNNs improves performance; (e) transfer learning from natural image datasets is a powerful method to improve the performance of CNN based CADe

i) CNN models with more than one hundred million parameters outperformed smaller networks in the LN detection task, and the performance of CNN models is not monotonically related to their number of parameters; ii) the scale of the dataset has a significant impact on the classification performance of deep CNNs, and the performance is not monotonously related to the scale of the training data; iii) the spatial context of the input images has an impact on the performance of deep CNN models; and iv

1) CNNs with 5 million to 10 million parameters are the most suitable models for medical image CAD tasks, 2) the spatial context of medical images is more critical to performance than the scale of training data, and 3) transfer learning from pre-trained ImageNet models is effective when there are not enough training data, or when the training data is not representative of the test data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
three important, but understudied factors in employing CNNs to medical imaging CAD tasks.
the following questions: What are the best CNN architectures for CADe?
how to best exploit the recent progress in deep learning to improve medical image analysis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CNNs are a powerful and promising tool for CAD, but the design and implementation of CNNs for medical imaging applications requires a careful consideration of the dataset and the task at hand.
CNN architectures are not the only factor that determines the performance of a CADe system.

(1) the CNN architectures are highly task and dataset dependent, and the performance is not always improved by adding layers; (2) the performance is not monotonically increased with the scale of the dataset; (3) the performance can be significantly improved by using transfer learning, but the performance gain is highly dependent on dataset size and task complexity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CNN architectures, training dataset scale, and the transfer learning technique all have important impacts on the CAD performance.
CNNs are very powerful for computer aided detection, and the best performance can be achieved by transfer learning from pre-trained CNNs on natural image datasets.
CNN architectures with more layers and parameters, more annotated training data, and fine tuning from pre trained CNN models can all lead to higher classification performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the performance of a CNN based CAD system can be significantly improved by exploiting the three factors we studied.
CNNs can be successfully applied to computer aided detection tasks, and that transfer learning from pre-trained ImageNet models is a powerful tool for CADe.
the CNN architectures with a large number of parameters and layers are more effective for computer aided detection problems than the smaller CNN architectures.
